verified_by: verify-authn-3 (adversarial re-audit of filed finding authn-3)

finding.title: Unauthenticated attacker can permanently lock the sole admin out of the console: username-keyed lockout with no per-IP limit, and failed_logins is never reset when the lock expires
finding.evidence: routes.go:42 `api.POST("/auth/login", s.login)` — no rate-limit middleware on the login route (quota.RateLimiter/RedisLimiter is gateway-API-key scoped only; quota/quota.go:55 `func (rl *RateLimiter) Allow(snap *runtime.Snapshot, apiKeyID uint, alias string)`). auth.go:76-79 `if err := bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword(...); err != nil { s.onMFAFail(&u); ... }` and auth.go:114-121 `func (s *Server) onMFAFail(u *model.AdminUser) { u.FailedLogins++; updates := map[string]any{"failed_logins": u.FailedLogins}; if u.FailedLogins >= 5 { loc := time.Now().Add(15 * time.Minute); updates["locked_until"] = loc } ... }`. model.go:28-30 `func (u *AdminUser) IsLocked() bool { return u.LockedUntil != nil && time.Now().Before(*u.LockedUntil) }` — the counter is cleared only by a successful login (auth.go:81-83) or POST /users/:id/unlock (users.go:61-62).
finding.impact: Lockout is keyed to the username, not the source address, so anyone on the network can spend the admin's 5 attempts with random passwords. Worse, because `failed_logins` stays at 5 after the 15-minute lock lapses, a single further wrong password immediately re-locks for another 15 minutes: a cron job sending one bogus password every ~15 minutes denies the legitimate admin access indefinitely. During a live incident this keeps the defender out of the console (cannot rotate provider keys, disable a leaked gateway key, or read audit) while the attacker's own session — see authn-2 — is unaffected. There is no per-IP throttle, no CAPTCHA and no alert on lock events to make this visible.
finding.mitigations_checked: lockout does exist and covers second-factor failures too (auth.go:67, auth.go:104 call onMFAFail), so TOTP brute force is throttled; an operator can clear it directly in the DB and /users/:id/unlock exists; SQLite `SetMaxOpenConns(1)` (db/db.go:52) serializes writes but does not prevent the cross-request state loss below.
finding.recommendation: Add a per-IP (and per-username+IP) token-bucket limiter in front of /auth/login, reset `failed_logins` when `locked_until` passes so the lock terminates the counter's life, and emit an alert/audit notification on lock events so an operator can distinguish an attack from a typo.

reason:
VERDICT: NOT refuted — the code fully supports the mechanism as filed; only the severity and one impact illustration are wrong, so the correct disposition is downgrade to medium.

1) EVIDENCE FIDELITY (all verbatim, all on the cited lines — no line drift found):
- backend/internal/admin/auth.go:114 is literally `func (s *Server) onMFAFail(u *model.AdminUser) {`; 115-121 are `u.FailedLogins++` / `updates := map[string]any{"failed_logins": u.FailedLogins}` / `if u.FailedLogins >= 5 {` / `loc := time.Now().Add(15 * time.Minute)` / `updates["locked_until"] = loc` / `s.db.Model(&model.AdminUser{}).Where("id = ?", u.ID).Updates(updates)`. Cited line 114 is accurate; no corrected_line needed.
- auth.go:76-79 wrong-password branch calls `s.onMFAFail(&u)` — i.e. the same handler named for MFA is what the *password* path uses, so a first-factor-only guess burns the counter with no other precondition.
- auth.go:67 and auth.go:104 confirm the second-factor branches also call onMFAFail (the finding's stated mitigation, TOTP throttling, is real).
- model.go:28-30 and users.go:61-62 (`Updates(map[string]any{"failed_logins": 0, "locked_until": nil})`) match exactly.
- routes.go:42 `api.POST("/auth/login", s.login)` — the only unauthenticated admin route with no handler-level guard; every sibling at routes.go:43+ carries `s.AuthMiddleware()`. middleware.go (read end-to-end, 33 lines) contains no limiter at all (its header comment '速率辅助' is stale).

2) CHAIN INTACT — no mitigation exists anywhere in the flow (each searched and confirmed absent):
- Engine level: main.go:89-118 registers only `gin.Recovery()`, the security-header closure, and an access-log closure. `srv := &http.Server{...}` (main.go:126) applies no connection/concurrency bound; `General.MaxConnections` is enforced only inside the gateway handler (gateway.go:195), never on /api/admin/v1.
- The limiter is provably gateway-only: quota/quota.go:33-36 `Limiter interface { Allow(snap *runtime.Snapshot, apiKeyID uint, alias string) ... }` keys windows as `ruleID:apiKeyID:alias` (quota.go:67) and the sole wiring is `gateway.New(gormDB, mgr, bl, rl, qm, al, mx)` (main.go:121); grep of the whole backend for rate-limit symbols finds no admin-side use, and redis_limiter.go:81 has the same apiKeyID/alias signature. Docs agree the Redis limiter is data-plane-only (README.md:52/257).
- No deployment-level throttle: grep for `limit_req|rate.?limit|fail2ban|iptables|max_conn` across all yml/yaml/conf/md/template/sh found only gateway/quota references — no nginx/LB config ships a login throttle.
- No operator knob: settings.Security (settings.go:79-84) has only MFAEnabled/MFARequiredAll/RecoveryCodeCount/GraceDays — the 5/15min values are hard-coded (auth.go:117-118), so a defender cannot widen the threshold, and there is no admin allowlist.
- No proactive alert: onMFAFail (auth.go:114-122) calls neither `recordOp` nor the only webhook path in the codebase (quota.go:216-223, quota-alerts only). Confirmed there is zero audit/notification on a lock event, as claimed.
- 'Never reset on expiry' is code-true, not inferred: a repo-wide grep for `FailedLogins|failed_logins|LockedUntil|locked_until|IsLocked` returns exactly 13 hits — auth.go:38, 81, 83, 115, 116, 117, 119, model.go:21-22, 28-29, users.go:27, 62. Nothing anywhere clears or expires the counter: `StartBackground` (quota.go:243-264) touches only quotas and limiter hits, and AutoMigrate (db.go:63) never rewrites admin_users state. So after the 15-minute lock lapses the row is still `failed_logins = 5` and one more bad password re-locks instantly.

3) THE RE-LOCK MECHANIC IS ACTUALLY *WORSE* THAN FILED (verified, strengthens the finding):
- auth.go:38-41 early-returns `40301 账户已被锁定` *before* onMFAFail, so attempts made while locked do not extend the lock — the lock always expires on schedule, and the attacker's next request (landing milliseconds later, since nothing throttles) re-arms another 15 minutes. With continuous hammering the unlocked window is effectively sub-millisecond: indefinite management-plane denial. Username discovery is not even required in stock config: config.go:65 `AdminUser: getenv("ADMIN_USER", "admin")` and bootstrapAdmin (main.go:164-183) create exactly that one account; a custom name is still confirmable by the same 403-vs-401 asymmetry already filed as authn-5.
- The finding was also *too generous* about its own mitigation: `/users/:id/unlock` cannot rescue this victim. routes.go:135 puts it behind `s.AuthMiddleware()`, and there is no user-creation route at all (routes.go:133-135 = GET /users, POST /users/:id/unbind-mfa, POST /users/:id/unlock; grep finds no `POST /users`), so the console can never grow a second administrator. The bootstrap account is the only account, and the only API that clears the lock requires a session of the account being denied. Real recovery is out-of-band SQL (`UPDATE admin_users SET failed_logins=0, locked_until=NULL`) or POST /backups/restore — which the locked-out operator cannot reach from the UI.

4) WHAT I DO CORRECT (basis of the downgrade, not of a refutation):
- The stated attack shape 'a cron job sending one bogus password every ~15 minutes denies the legitimate admin access indefinitely' does not hold as written. Under 1 attempt / 15 min the account is unlocked for essentially the whole interval, and a single successful login runs auth.go:81-83 (`u.FailedLogins = 0` + `Update("failed_logins", 0)`) which returns the budget to 5. Indefinite denial requires *continuous* guessing — which the absence of any throttle makes trivial, so the conclusion survives but the premise must be restated.
- 'No alert ... to make this visible' is true only for *proactive* visibility. The victim is not entirely blind: HTTP 403 carries `body.message`, and client.ts:79-80 (`if (bizMessage) { message.error(bizMessage) }`) surfaces '账户已被锁定…' in the UI (Login.tsx:66-70 then contradicts it with an extra 'network error' toast, since its 401/40101/40102/40103 test misses 403/40301). Operator discovery is still purely passive — they must already be trying to log in — which is why the availability loss can persist unnoticed, but 'invisible' overstates it.
- The dangling 'cross-request state loss' in mitigations_checked refers to authn-4's non-atomic read-modify-write, not to anything in authn-3; that race makes the lockout *harder* to trigger (a concurrent burst advances the counter by ~1), so it does not support this finding and should be dropped from its narrative. It does not break the chain either: with unbounded attempts, extra requests simply compensate.

5) SEVERITY RATING UNDER THIS ENGAGEMENT'S TAXONOMY:
- Not critical: no unauthenticated RCE, no authz bypass, no data exfiltration — the attacker gains no credential, no session and no read of any secret.
- Not high: the stated bar is 'authed-but-severe or account takeover'. This is an unauthenticated *availability* impairment of the *management plane only*, and it is provably confined to that plane: gateway/ contains zero references to `AdminUser`/`failed_logins`, so LLM traffic, routing, guardrails and billing keep running while the console is locked. Recovery is a single SQL UPDATE (or stopping the hammering plus one successful login), i.e. fully reversible with no integrity or confidentiality loss.
- Medium is the exact fit: 'defense-in-depth gap with real impact'. It is a genuine implementation bug (a lock that never disarms its own counter, plus a recovery API that is unreachable for the only victim), with real, easily-triggered, persistent impact — above low/hygiene, below the high bar. Aggravating context worth noting (and why it still does not reach high): it degrades incident response exactly when the operator needs to rotate a leaked provider key or disable a stolen gateway key, and it compounds authn-2 (a live attacker session survives the lockout entirely). Recommendation as filed is correct and should be kept: per-IP + per-(username,IP) token bucket in front of /auth/login; treat lock expiry as the end of the counter's life (reset `failed_logins` when `locked_until` is in the past — e.g. lazily at the auth.go:38 check, which also avoids needing a sweeper job); move the failure counter into the existing shared mfaStore (Redis INCR+EXPIRE where configured); make the thresholds configurable in settings.Security; log+alert on the transition into locked state; and expose an unlock path that does not require a session of the account being unlocked.
exploit_sketch:
Target: stock single-node deployment, admin console reachable over HTTP (bind is `:%d` on all interfaces, main.go:126), username 'admin' (config.go:65), MFA off or on — neither matters for the first factor.

Step 1 — burn the 5 attempts (unauthenticated, no throttle):
  for i in $(seq 1 5); do curl -s -X POST http://TARGET:8080/api/admin/v1/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"admin","password":"wrong-'$i'"}'; done
  → 5x HTTP 401 {"code":40102}; auth.go:76-79 → onMFAFail → failed_logins=5 → auth.go:117-119 sets locked_until = now+15m.

Step 2 — confirm the lock (auth.go:38-41, no credential needed):
  curl -si -X POST .../auth/login -d '{"username":"admin","password":"x"}'
  → HTTP 403 {"code":40301,"message":"账户已被锁定，请稍后再试或联系管理员解锁"}
  (Attempts inside this window return 403 before onMFAFail, so the lock is not extended — it lapses on schedule.)

Step 3 — the sticky re-lock (this is the bug that makes the DoS permanent):
  # t = +15:00.001, first request after expiry finds IsLocked()==false (model.go:29) but failed_logins still 5
  curl -s -X POST .../auth/login -d '{"username":"admin","password":"x"}'   # 1 request
  → auth.go:115 `u.FailedLogins++` → 6 → `>= 5` → brand-new 15-minute lock.
  Loop steps 2-3 (or just keep POSTing wrong passwords once per second in one thread) and the account is locked ~100% of wall-clock time; each expiry is re-armed within milliseconds, so the legitimate admin's correct credentials always hit the 403 branch at auth.go:38 and can never reach the reset at auth.go:81-83.

Step 4 — no self-service recovery exists:
  GET .../api/admin/v1/users → 401 (routes.go:133 requires JWT); POST .../users/1/unlock → 401 (routes.go:135) — the only API that clears `locked_until` is gated behind the session of the very account being denied, and no route can create a second admin. Operator must shell-edit SQLite (`UPDATE admin_users SET failed_logins=0, locked_until=NULL WHERE id=1;`) or restore a backup; restarting the process does not help (state is persistent).

Step 5 — cover/noise: nothing records the lockout (onMFAFail performs no `recordOp`), so the operator audit trail shows no failed logins and no lock events at all; meanwhile the attacker's pre-existing 24h JWT (authn-2) keeps full admin access, and gateway traffic (`/v1/*` with `sk-` keys) is entirely unaffected.
additional_verified_notes: routes.go:133-135 + no POST /users anywhere: the admin console structurally supports exactly one bootstrap account unless an operator hand-inserts rows into SQLite, so the '/users/:id/unlock exists' mitigation counted in the original finding is unreachable for the sole victim — this aggravates rather than refutes the finding.

client.ts:79-80 leaks the raw 403/40301 lock message as a toast while Login.tsx:66-70 additionally prints 'network error' (its branch test omits 403/40301): the intended anti-enumeration suppression in the UI is defeated by the interceptor, and the victim receives contradictory diagnostics.
middleware.go:1 header comment claims the file provides '速率辅助' (rate helpers); the 33-line file contains only JWT parsing. There is no admin-side rate helper anywhere in backend/.

Data plane isolation verified: grep of backend/internal/gateway for AdminUser/failed_logins → no matches, so an admin lockout cannot interrupt routed LLM traffic. This is why the impact is management-plane availability, not service-wide outage.
